content_text: [1/4 @gregoryblotnick] 2nd most important lesson I learned in my 30's you'll get a far more accurate view of someone's character, by viewing a human being -- any human being -- simply as a pile of as virtues and vices. this all ties into critical thinking, objectivity, removing emotion and preconceived biases from how u navigate life. (1/6) - Feelings > Thoughts we are hardwired to "feel" about people. we dont really think, no human has ever been rational. our mind says "I like that guy" or "I don't like that guy," and then we bucket them as good or bad and make excuses for their behavior unfortunately, even the people u loathe have some redeeming qualities to them its like that meme: "when the worst person you know makes a good point" you want to be able to recognize that. (2/6) - Objectivity > Subjectivity everything is about assessing people's virtues and vices, from a purely objective standpoint excellent Kierkegaard quote that sums this up: "Most men are subjective toward themselves and objective toward all others, frightfully objective sometimes – but the task is precisely to be objective toward oneself and subjective toward all others.” this is why TDS is so deadly, and as many great investors have commented, its bewildering to watch money managers fall so deeply into it the entire job is based around removing cognitive, emotional, and mental biases and thus, by being so open about refusing to acknowledge a single virtue -- when every human who has ever lived has at least one -- the crowd is correct in straightlining this "syndrome" to one's investing ability, or lack thereof. I have no strong view on the man, but I'll be damned if I ever let a single human occupy even .01% of the mental real estate that he takes up for half this country. (3/6) - How To Do This, Except 100% Wrong Ditto for the stoic guy that everyone is getting on -- the crowd is correct in saying "wtf?" You prize yourself on emotional self-discipline and equanimity and a powerful mind that withstands the influence of all passions, and then visibly lose your shit because you don't like the President? Seneca would call you "woman'ish" and effeminate, you really can't hold yourself up as a champion of some philosophy that you clearly don't even practice. But I don't want to talk about the President, its just a perfect example of what this tweet is supposed to look like... except the complete opposite. We want 100% objectivity, 0% subjectivity. These are examples of 100% subjectivity, 0% objectivity. All new information is processed through the "orange man bad" filter in a way that seems to remove any possibility of objective, rational analysis. Purely subjective, purely based on preconceived notions. No action is good or bad; if he did it, its bad, if not, its good. So take all of this, and use it as an example of what not to do. (4/6) - Compiling The Dictionary The first step to shifting your worldview towards virtues/vices, requires a mental dictionary of what all those are. The full list, the shopping cart, all the characteristics that could potentially assemble like Megazord to form a human being. God leaves no one empty-handed, on both ends. I have never met a human that didn't have several redeeming qualities, whether I wanted to admit it or not. The crowd is assertive in searching for vices in great men, but fails to assign virtues where due. Chalk it up to envy and pride and vanity and arrogance, the inherent human desire to say "I'm better than you." But for your own self-interest, you want to be able to recognize, tag, and absorb these traits as you see them displayed in people...inculcate the virtues you like, while avoiding or mitigating the vices. (5/6) - Give All Men Their Due This will make you a much more forgiving human, probably more pleasant to be around, and it allows you to treat every interaction as one that you can learn something from. You'll either want their virtues, or you'll want to avoid their vices -- there's something for everybody. And in viewing people through an objective lens, or as close to objective as possible, you'll free yourself from emotion, and you'll stop lazily tagging people as "good" or "bad." There's never been a good man or a bad man; just ones with more virtues than vices, or more vices than virtues. Give people their due, and more importantly, become an astute, critical, and articulate evaluator of the traits that comprise a single human's character. (6/6) - Case Study: Napoleon Example to drive this home Napoleon is one of the most-written-about humans ever, with estimates as high as 300,000 books that are about him + his empire. We have tons of primary material. We probably know as much about him as any human who has ever lived. So we should probably have a definitive answer to this question: "Was Napoleon a good dude or a bad dude" The answer? There is no answer. It depends who you ask, on the biographer's opinion, and on his cherry-picked selection of primary material to prove his point. We only have opinions. So if we can't say "good or bad" about Napoleon Bonaparte -- a man we know more about than just about anyone, aside from Jesus Christ -- what makes you think you have any more certainty on some random beta cuck from X dot com? This is why with Napoleon and any other character, or biographical case study, we just want break him down into virtues and vices. Mimic the virtues, and avoid the vices. END: A Final Wrinkle The final step is one that we can sum up in Napoleon's own words: "Du sublime au ridicule, il n'y a qu'un pas." From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step. What is the step? That a man's virtues and vices tend to be inseparable. They are two sides of the same coin. You can't just clip the vice and keep the virtue -- it's as if they are tied together at the tail. "A man's greatest weakness, is often his greatest strength taken too far." This adds an entirely new level of complexity to the whole framework, but I'd be remiss not to point it out, if only for your own benefit as you try to rationally assess your own strengths and weaknesses. Nietzsche's framing of willpower is how he ties this all together. All great men, the heroes and the villians, possess an incredible quantum of willpower. This quantum makes them capable of inflicting great good, or great evil, upon the world. The way the cookie crumbled, could have gone entirely the other way. But they possessed some trait, both vice and virtue, that allowed them to shape the world as they saw fit. And just because they chose one direction, doesn't mean they weren't capable of the other. That's the link between vice and virtue, and that's why La Rochefoucauld opened his "Maximes" -- one of the best books ever written on human nature -- with this legendary banger: "Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised." --- [2/4 @stalmico] @gregoryblotnick this applies so well to evaluating cofounders --- [3/4 @Ascent_Cap] @gregoryblotnick thanks Blotnick, you’re my fav follow on X --- [4/4 @gregoryblotnick] @Ascent_Cap 🫡
